transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A new study has found that practicing mindfulness meditation regularly can significantly reduce stress and anxiety and improve mental health, according to researchers at Harvard University. The study followed over 400 adults over an 8-week period and found that those who practiced mindfulness meditation for about 30 minutes a day showed significant reductions in stress, anxiety, and symptoms of depression compared to those who didn't meditate. Brain scans also showed changes in brain regions associated with emotion regulation and self-awareness. Mindfulness meditation involves focusing your attention on the present moment and accepting it without judgment. Researchers say that meditation is like exercise for the brain—it strengthens areas of the brain involved in attention and emotional control, and it can be a simple, low-cost way to improve mental health.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

2. What is mindfulness meditation?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: The city of London is expanding its network of "quiet ways"—bicycle routes on quieter, less-trafficked streets that are designed to make cycling safer and more appealing to people who don't normally ride bikes. Unlike traditional bike lanes that are on busy roads, quiet ways use side streets and residential roads, with traffic calming measures like speed bumps and reduced speed limits to make them safer and more comfortable for cyclists. The goal is to create a network of safe, pleasant cycling routes across the city that connect residential areas with workplaces, shops, and public transportation. The city says that increasing cycling will reduce traffic congestion, improve air quality, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and improve public health. The quiet ways program is part of London's plan to become a zero-carbon city by 2030.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Researchers have developed a new artificial intelligence system that can diagnose eye diseases as accurately as human doctors, according to a new study published in Nature Medicine. The AI system was trained on thousands of eye scans to detect signs of diabetic retinopathy, a common complication of diabetes that can lead to blindness if not caught early. In tests, the system was able to identify patients with the disease with about 94 percent accuracy, which is comparable to expert ophthalmologists. Researchers say that AI could help address the shortage of eye doctors in many parts of the world, especially in rural and low-income areas where access to specialists is limited. The technology is still being tested, but researchers hope it could eventually be used to screen patients for eye diseases quickly and affordably.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Jack): Hey, I'm planning a trip to Scotland this summer. Have you ever been?
Woman (Emma): Oh, I love Scotland! I went there two years ago and it was amazing. The scenery is absolutely beautiful.
Man: Great! I'm so excited. I'm planning to spend about two weeks there. Do you have any recommendations? Where should I go?

Woman: Well, you should definitely spend a few days in Edinburgh. It's such a beautiful city—full of history, with the castle, the Old Town, the Royal Mile... there's so much to see and do. And if you're there in August, there's the Fringe Festival, which is the biggest arts festival in the world.
Man: Yeah, I've heard about that. I'm actually going in July, so I'll miss the festival, but that's okay. I want to see the countryside too. Where else should I go?

Woman: Oh, you have to go to the Highlands! That's the best part, in my opinion. The scenery is just stunning—mountains, lochs, valleys... it's like something out of a movie. You can drive the North Coast 500, which is a scenic route around the north coast of Scotland. It's about 500 miles long, and it's absolutely beautiful.
Man: That sounds amazing. I was thinking about renting a car and driving around. Is that a good idea?

Woman: Definitely! Renting a car is the best way to see the Highlands. Public transportation is pretty limited outside of the cities, so having a car gives you a lot more freedom. Just be prepared for narrow roads and sheep in the road.
Man: Ha, okay. What about weather? I've heard it rains a lot in Scotland.

Woman: Yeah, it can rain a lot, even in summer. And the weather can change really quickly—one minute it's sunny, the next it's pouring. So make sure you bring layers and a good waterproof jacket. And waterproof shoes, too.
Man: Got it. What about food? What's Scottish food like? I've heard about haggis, but I'm not sure if I want to try that.

Woman: Ha, haggis is definitely an acquired taste. But there's lots of other great food too. Scotland has amazing seafood—fresh fish, salmon, oysters... And they have great meat, like lamb and beef. And you have to try a full Scottish breakfast! It's like an English breakfast but with haggis and black pudding.
Man: Hmm, maybe I'll try haggis just to say I did. What about whiskey? I know Scotland is famous for whiskey.

Woman: Oh, definitely! You should visit a whiskey distillery while you're there. There are hundreds of them all over Scotland, especially in the Highlands and on islands like Islay. You can take a tour, learn how whiskey is made, and do a tasting. It's really interesting.
Man: That sounds great. I'll have to do that. Is there anything else I should know?

Woman: Let's see... the people are really friendly, especially in the smaller towns. And Scotland has such a rich history and culture—castles, ancient monuments, traditional music... there's so much to explore.
Man: Awesome. I'm even more excited now. Thanks for all the tips, Emma.
Woman: No problem! You're going to have an amazing time. Let me know how it goes when you get back.
Man: I will. Thanks again!
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What does Emma say about getting around the Highlands?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (David): Hey, I've been thinking about getting a dog. What do you think?
Woman (Sarah): A dog? That's a big decision. Are you sure you're ready for that? Dogs are a lot of work.
Man: I know, but I've been wanting one for a long time. I live alone and I feel like a dog would be good company. And it would make me get more exercise, which would be good for me.
Woman: Yeah, those are good reasons. But you have to think about it carefully. Dogs are a 10 to 15 year commitment. Are you ready for that?
Man: I think so. I'm pretty responsible. But I am a little worried about my work schedule. I work 9 to 5, five days a week. Is that too long for a dog to be alone?

Woman: Hmm, that's a good question. Most dogs shouldn't be left alone for more than 4 to 6 hours at a time, especially puppies. If you're gone for 8 or 9 hours a day, that could be a problem. Dogs are social animals and they can get lonely and bored.
Man: Yeah, that's what I was worried about. What can I do? I can't quit my job.

Woman: Well, there are options. You could hire a dog walker to come in the middle of the day and take the dog out. Or you could take the dog to doggy daycare a few days a week. Or if you have a friend or neighbor who's home during the day, maybe they could help.
Man: Those are good ideas. A dog walker might be expensive, though. How much does that usually cost?
Woman: It depends on where you live, but usually around $15 to $20 for a 30-minute walk. It adds up, but it's worth it if it means the dog is happy and healthy.
Man: Yeah. What kind of dog do you think I should get? I was thinking maybe a golden retriever or a labrador. They seem like nice dogs.

Woman: Golden retrievers and labs are great dogs—friendly, smart, good with people. But they're also high-energy dogs that need a lot of exercise. If you don't have a lot of time to exercise them, they might not be the best choice.
Man: Hmm, good point. What about a smaller dog? Like a French bulldog or something? Do they need less exercise?

Woman: Yeah, smaller dogs generally need less exercise. But French bulldogs can have health problems, especially breathing problems, because of their flat faces. And they can be pretty expensive to buy.
Man: Oh, right. I've heard about that. What about adopting from a shelter instead of buying from a breeder?

Woman: Oh, I think adopting is a great idea! There are so many dogs in shelters that need good homes. And shelter dogs are often already house-trained and know basic commands. And it's a lot cheaper than buying from a breeder.
Man: Yeah, I like that idea. I could give a dog a second chance. What do I need to do to prepare?

Woman: Well, you'll need to puppy-proof your house—make sure there's nothing dangerous the dog can get into. You'll need food, bowls, a bed, a leash, a collar, toys... And you should find a good vet before you get the dog.
Man: Okay, that makes sense. And how much does it cost to have a dog, roughly?

Woman: It depends, but probably around $1,000 to $2,000 a year for food, vet bills, toys, and other supplies. And that's not including unexpected vet bills, which can be expensive. You might want to consider pet insurance.
Man: Wow, that's more than I thought. But I think I can afford it. Let me think about it some more.
Woman: Yeah, take your time. It's a big decision. But if you're ready, a dog can be an amazing companion.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The history of the bicycle is a story of innovation and evolution that spans over 200 years. From the earliest wooden walking machines to the modern, lightweight, high-tech bicycles we know today, the bicycle has changed a lot, but its basic purpose—providing simple, efficient human-powered transportation—has remained the same.

The earliest ancestor of the bicycle was the "draisine" or "running machine," invented by Karl von Drais in Germany in 1817. It was made entirely of wood, had two wheels, and you propelled it by pushing your feet against the ground, like a modern balance bike. It didn't have pedals or brakes.

In the 1860s, the first bicycles with pedals were invented in France. These were called "boneshakers" because they had wooden wheels with iron tires, which made for a very bumpy, uncomfortable ride. But they were faster and more efficient than the draisine.

The 1870s and 1880s saw the rise of the "penny-farthing" or "high-wheel" bicycle, which had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. The large front wheel allowed the bike to go farther with each pedal stroke, making it faster. But it was also dangerous—if you hit a bump or stopped too suddenly, you could go flying over the handlebars. And because you sat so high up, falls could be serious.

The modern bicycle as we know it was invented in the 1880s with the "safety bicycle." The safety bicycle had two wheels of equal size, a chain drive to power the back wheel, and pneumatic (air-filled) tires, which made for a much smoother, more comfortable ride. It was called the "safety" bicycle because it was much safer and easier to ride than the penny-farthing.

The safety bicycle was a huge success, and it started a bicycle craze in the 1890s. Bicycles became popular with people of all classes, and they had a big impact on society. They gave people more freedom and mobility, especially women, who had previously been more limited in how far they could travel. The bicycle also played a role in the women's rights movement.

Since then, bicycles have continued to evolve, with improvements in materials, gears, brakes, and design. Today, there are many different types of bicycles for different purposes—road bikes, mountain bikes, hybrid bikes, electric bikes, and more. But the basic design of the safety bicycle has remained largely unchanged for over 130 years, which is a testament to how well it works.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: Animals communicate with each other in many different and fascinating ways. While humans primarily use language to communicate, animals use a wide variety of signals—sounds, body language, smells, colors, and even electrical signals—to convey information to each other. Understanding how animals communicate can teach us a lot about their behavior, their social lives, and even about the evolution of communication itself.

One of the most well-known examples of animal communication is the honeybee's waggle dance. When a forager bee finds a good source of food, it returns to the hive and performs a special dance that tells the other bees where the food is. The direction and length of the dance convey information about the direction and distance of the food source. It's a remarkably sophisticated form of communication for such a small animal.

Many animals use sound to communicate. Birds sing to attract mates and defend their territories. Whales and dolphins use complex vocalizations to communicate with each other over long distances underwater. Elephants use low-frequency sounds that can travel for many kilometers through the ground to communicate with other elephants far away. And frogs croak to attract mates and establish territory.

Body language is another important form of communication for many animals. Dogs wag their tails when they're happy and tuck their tails between their legs when they're scared or submissive. Cats purr when they're content and arch their backs and hiss when they're angry or scared. Primates like chimpanzees and gorillas use a wide range of facial expressions, gestures, and body postures to communicate with each other.

Many animals also use chemical signals to communicate. Ants leave pheromone trails to guide other ants to food sources. Many mammals use scent marking to establish territory and communicate with other members of their species. And some animals can even detect chemical signals from predators and respond accordingly.

Some animals use visual signals for communication. Many birds have bright, colorful plumage that they use to attract mates. Chameleons change color to communicate their mood and to blend in with their surroundings. And fireflies use bioluminescence—glowing—to attract mates.

Animal communication is incredibly diverse and complex, and scientists are still learning new things about it all the time. Studying how animals communicate can help us understand how our own language and communication evolved, and it can also help us better understand and protect the animals we share our planet with.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges facing the world today. The Earth's climate is changing at an unprecedented rate, with rising temperatures, melting ice caps, rising sea levels, and more frequent and intense extreme weather events. Understanding what causes climate change, what its effects are, and what we can do about it is essential for building a sustainable future.

The main cause of current climate change is the greenhouse effect. The greenhouse effect is a natural process where certain gases in the atmosphere—like carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor—trap heat from the sun, keeping the Earth warm enough to live on. Without the greenhouse effect, the Earth would be too cold for life. But human activities—especially burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas—are increasing the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which is trapping more heat and causing the Earth to warm up faster than it naturally would.

Burning fossil fuels for electricity, transportation, and industry is the biggest source of greenhouse gas emissions. Deforestation—cutting down forests for agriculture or development—also contributes to climate change, because trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and when they're cut down, that carbon is released back into the air. Agriculture, especially livestock farming, is another major source of emissions, particularly methane.

The effects of climate change are already being felt around the world. Global temperatures have risen by about 1.1 degrees Celsius since the pre-industrial era. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting, causing sea levels to rise, which threatens coastal communities with flooding and erosion. Extreme weather events like hurricanes, heatwaves, droughts, and wildfires are becoming more frequent and more intense. And climate change is affecting ecosystems and biodiversity, putting many species at risk of extinction.

But climate change isn't inevitable—there are things we can do to address it. Reducing our greenhouse gas emissions is the most important thing. This means transitioning from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources like solar, wind, and hydro power. It means making our buildings more energy efficient. It means improving public transportation and reducing our reliance on cars. And it means changing our consumption habits and reducing waste.

We also need to adapt to the changes that are already happening and that are unavoidable. This means building sea walls and flood defenses to protect coastal communities, developing more drought-resistant crops, and preparing for more extreme weather events.

Addressing climate change requires action at all levels—from individuals to governments to international organizations. It's a complex and challenging problem, but it's not hopeless. With the right policies, technologies, and changes in behavior, we can reduce our emissions and build a more sustainable future.
